FilmTaxation_B

In a fictional French-speaking country, Hollywood films and Domestically produced films are modelled as two separate and independent markets. Quantity is measured in millions of cinema tickets, and monetary surplus is measured in millions.

Consumers belong to either Group A or Group B. Each group has one demand curve in each market. Demand for one type of film is unaffected by the other type of film's market. Each market's aggregate demand demand is obtained by adding the two group demands. Each group's consumer surplus is the sum of its consumer surplus in the two markets.

The Hollywood-film competitive equilibrium is given by: price 144; total tickets 2055; producer surplus 0; Group A consumer surplus 34564; Group B consumer surplus 151899.

Question 1 [1.5]  

Show that the competitive equilibrium quantity in the Domestic-film market is 1404, and give the price and quantities purchased by each group.

Answer
[1.5]  

The market demand curve is the horizontal sum of the two group demands. The Domestic competitive equilibrium has price approximately 199 and quantity approximately 1404. Group A purchases approximately 1120 tickets and Group B approximately 284.

Question 2 [1.0]  

The government imposes a tax of 35 per Hollywood ticket. Explain the incidence of the tax.

Answer
[1.0]  

Hollywood supply is perfectly elastic. The producer price remains 144, while the consumer price rises to 179; consumers therefore bear the entire tax. The fictional country is small relative to the global Hollywood market, so its market and policies do not affect the Hollywood supply curve.

Question 3 [1.5]  

The government decides to use the tax revenue to subsidise each Domestic-film ticket by 51. A report commissioned by the Culture Minister projects tax revenue of 35 × 2055 = 71925 and subsidy expenditure of 51 × 1404 = 71604, and claims that the scheme will be balanced (and actually run a small net revenue). Discuss.

Answer
[1.5]  

The projected balance is 71604 - 71925 = 321. Relative to flows of roughly 71938, that difference can reasonably be treated as rounding or graphical approximation.

The substantive mistake is using competitive-equilibrium quantities without accounting for the fact that the policy changes incentives. The tax will make Hollywood sales fall and Domestic sales rise, to the Culture Minister is both under-estimating the expenditure and over-estimating the revenue.

Question 4 [1.5]  

Call policy M the package of a tax of 35 per Hollywood ticket and a subsidy of 38 per Domestic ticket. Find the M equilibrium in each market. Show that the budget is balanced, up to rounding errors.

Answer
[1.5]  

Under M, the Hollywood consumer price is approximately 179, the producer price is 144, and quantity is approximately 1850. The Domestic consumer price is approximately 179, the producer price is approximately 217, and quantity is approximately 1716.

Tax revenue is approximately 64753 and subsidy expenditure approximately 64753, up to rounding errors.

Question 5 [1.5]  

Find and interpret the deadweight loss from policy M across both markets.

Answer
[1.5]  

Hollywood-market deadweight loss is approximately 3593. It is the value of mutually beneficial Hollywood-ticket transactions prevented by the tax q = 1850 through q = 2055, which would each produce a total surplus of v(q) - c(q), where v(.) is the marginal WTP on the aggregate demand curve, and c(q) is the marginal cost, on the supply curve, so the DWL is ∫ v(q) - c(q), q=1850..2055. Graphically, this is the Md Ms C triangle.

Domestic-market deadweight loss is approximately 5247. It is the value of transactions with negative surplus, which cost more to supply than viewers are willing to pay, q = 1404 through q = 1716, These units would each produce a total surplus of v(q) - c(q) < 0, so the DWL is ∫ c(q) - v(q), q=1404..1716. Graphically, this is the Md Ms C polygon.

Total deadweight loss is the sum of both markets' DWL: 8840.

You could find the domestic DWL via graphical surplus accounting instead.

In the competitive equilibrium C:
CS = A283 C O199
PS = S115 C O199
TW = S115 C A283

In the subsidised equilibrium M:
CS = A283 Md O180
PS = S115 Ms O218
or, better for graphical accounting,
PS = Z77 Md O180
GS = - Z77 Md Ms S115
For total welfare in M, we need to add up positive areas and negative areas:
Z77 S115 S180 Md counts positively in PS, negatively in GS, cancelling out
S180 C Md counts positively in CS, negatively in GS, cancelling out
S115 C A283 counts positively
Md Ms C counts negatively
Hence, TW(M) = (S115 C A283) - (Md Ms C).
Since TW(C) = (S115 C A283), DWL(M) = TW(C)-TW(M) = (Md Ms C).

Question 6 [1.5]  

Call policy S the package of a tax of 80 per Hollywood ticket and a subsidy of 62 per Domestic ticket. Find the S equilibrium in each market. Show that the budget is balanced, up to rounding errors.

Answer
[1.5]  

Under S, the Hollywood consumer price is approximately 224, the producer price is 144, and quantity is approximately 1406. The Domestic consumer price is approximately 160, the producer price is approximately 222, and quantity is approximately 1805.

Tax revenue is approximately 112465 and subsidy expenditure approximately 112465.

Question 7 [2.0]  

Who benefits and who loses from the transition M → S? Quantify their stakes, including their collective willingness to pay to enact or block the transition. Explain.

Answer
[2.0]  

From M to S, Group A's consumer surplus changes by approximately +5995, Group B's by -48452, and Domestic producer surplus by +9371.

Group A and Domestic producers form a coalition of net beneficiaries from the transition. Their collective gain, and their collective willingness to pay to enact the transition, is approximately 15366. Group B's collective willingness to pay to block the transition is approximately 48452.

Question 8 [1.5]  

On Twitter, @Mark and @Kris are arguing about the policy:

@Mark: Why exactly are we subsidising a bunch of Domestic films no one wants to see? And why are we punishing people who watch Hollywood films? The last Domestic film I saw was so bad, I haven't been to a cinema in months and I'm not planning to go back.

@Kris: Why are you complaining? You don't even watch films, so the tax does not affect you. And think of the 40,000 people who work in the film industry. This is their livelihood!

Critically assess Mark and Kris's discussion. Use no more than four concise bullet points.

Answer
[1.5]  
  • Mark's claim that no one wants the additional Domestic films misstates deadweight loss. Viewers may have positive willingness to pay, but the subsidised marginal tickets cost more to supply than viewers are willing to pay.
  • Someone who buys no Hollywood tickets after the tax can still be affected: the tax may have prevented purchases that would otherwise have generated consumer surplus.
  • The 40,000 jobs are not an additional social benefit. Labour and other production inputs have opportunity costs.
  • The policy can transfer surplus to Domestic producers and workers, but those distributional gains do not remove the deadweight loss created across the two markets.
